\subsection{Scores and breach behavior answer different questions}

Accuracy rankings leave breach behavior unresolved: the matched FX gain coexists with more breaches before calibration (Table~\ref{tab:fx}). Pinball loss measures error amounts while a strict-hit indicator records event occurrence, so monitoring reports should show both forms of error.

Elementary-score rankings cross for both original main comparisons (Supplement Figures S2--S3, Section S33). A separate 24-step FX comparison against rolling translated paths reverses near 20.6:1. Both six-step FX comparisons reduce mean underprediction and mean overprediction, so the weight reversal belongs specifically to the 24-step reference.

Loss and hit diagnostics answer different questions (Supplement Table S47, Section S33). HAC tests compare average loss and strict-hit tests examine event frequency and serial behavior, while RMS-state diagnostics compare conditional predictive ability across training-defined groups \citep{gw2006}.

\subsection{Why does regression lose at low frequency?}\label{sec:v12-low-frequency}
Penalty selection dominates positive excess loss in 27 of 41 short-history weekly comparisons (Figure~\ref{fig:v12-decomposition}). Extending validation lowers CFTC median excess loss from 19.33\% to 4.03\% with short histories, and from 10.35\% to 0.53\% with longer histories. The New York Fed medians fall from 6.68\% to -1.13\% at horizon six and from 40.47\% to 5.02\% at horizon twenty-four (Table~\ref{tab:v13-validation}). Yet the best finite penalty selected with evaluation hindsight still loses to historical headroom in 29 of 41 comparisons. This residual gap indicates limited incremental information within the tested feature set and finite menu.
